screens.title: Amazon DynamoDB — NoSQL Database for Developers
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore Amazon DynamoDB from a developer's point of view. We'll build a clear mental model: DynamoDB stores tables of items made of attributes and uses primary keys to find data quickly. You'll learn why DynamoDB is schema-less, when that flexibility helps, and why choosing the right partition key prevents performance issues. We'll also cover how the AWS SDK performs basic create, read, update and delete operations, and how capacity—read and write units—affects cost and throttling. For example, you will see how a Products table can store different attributes per item without breaking queries, and how using a user identifier plus timestamp supports efficient event retrieval. We'll contrast on-demand capacity and provisioned RCUs/WCUs so you understand operational trade-offs. By the end of the chapter you will be able to model a simple table, perform CRUD with Boto3, and spot common design mistakes like low-cardinality keys that create hot partitions. Consider what access patterns your app needs before you choose a primary key; that choice will guide your entire design.

screens.title: DynamoDB Fundamentals: Tables, Items, Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the core building blocks of DynamoDB so you can map application objects to storage. A table is a container for items. An item is a collection of attributes; think of an item as a document or a row whose attributes can vary from item to item. DynamoDB is schema-less, which means you do not need to define every attribute up front. This flexibility lets you add fields for some items without altering the entire table. However, it also shifts responsibility to you: design your access patterns so important attributes are present where queries expect them. The primary key uniquely identifies each item. If you use a single partition key, DynamoDB hashes its value to choose a storage partition. With a composite primary key—partition and sort—you group related items by partition and order them by the sort key, enabling efficient range queries. A common example is user events: a UserID partition key and a Timestamp sort key let you fetch recent events in chronological order. A misconception is thinking schema-less means structure-free; you still need consistent keys and predictable access paths. What part of your data needs ordered access, and which fields will vary per item?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tables hold items; items hold attributes. Schema-less design provides flexibility but requires intentional key and access-pattern planning.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Tables & Items
Key terms
Table
A named container for items. Use tables to group related items for an application domain, like Products or Orders.
Item
A single data record identified by a primary key. Items can have different attributes from one another.
Attribute
A name-value pair within an item. Attributes are analogous to columns but are optional and flexible per item.
Example
# Example item in a Products table
{
  'ProductId': 'P001',
  'Name': 'Laptop',
  'Price': 1200.00,
  'Status': 'Available'
}
Key Takeaway
Treat DynamoDB as a document store where structure is flexible, but keys are rigid and must be planned.
Common Mistake
Assuming schema-less means query-free: without consistent keys and attributes, queries become unreliable.
Analogy
Think of the table as a bookshelf and items as books. Each book can have different chapters and notes, but every book has an ISBN that uniquely identifies it.
Why it matters
Flexible attributes reduce schema migrations, but you must keep keys stable to ensure efficient, predictable queries.
Check your understanding
Name one attribute you would make optional in a product item and one attribute that must always be present for queries.

screens.title: Choosing Primary Keys and Avoiding Hot Partitions
screens.narratorSegment: Primary keys define how DynamoDB stores and finds items, so choosing them is a design decision with operational consequences. When you use a partition key alone, DynamoDB applies an internal hash to the key value to determine the physical partition. This works best when key values are high-cardinality and evenly distributed. With a composite key—partition plus sort—you group related items under the same partition and order them by the sort key, which enables efficient range queries such as retrieving a user's activities by timestamp. A common mistake is picking a low-cardinality partition key such as a fixed status value, which funnels traffic to a few partitions and causes hot partitions. Hot partitions lead to throttling and uneven performance. To choose keys, follow a simple process: first list your access patterns; second identify attributes used to retrieve related sets of items; third prefer attributes with many distinct values for the partition key; fourth use sort keys to support ordered queries or multiple items per partition. For example, to fetch all orders for a customer in order date, choose CustomerID as partition and OrderDate as sort. Reflect on your app: which queries require grouping, and which require single-item lookup?

keyIdea.title: Primary key strategy
keyIdea.text: Pick high-cardinality partition keys to spread load and use sort keys for grouping and ordered queries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Primary Keys
Key selection process
A repeatable sequence to map access patterns to key design.
1
List access patterns
Write queries your app must support. Start from what you will fetch most often.
2
Pick partition attribute
Choose a high-cardinality attribute for even distribution. Example: UserID or ProductId.
3
Use sort key for grouping
Add a sort key like Timestamp to order items within a partition for efficient ranges.
4
Validate for hotspots
Simulate or estimate traffic for hot values. Rework the key if a few values receive disproportionate traffic.
Example
Design an Orders table to query all orders for a customer by date: CustomerID as partition key, OrderDate as sort key. This returns ordered results with a single Query call.
Hot partition anti-pattern
Using a static or low-cardinality attribute like ORDER_STATUS as a partition key sends most requests to a few partitions. This causes throttling and poor latency.
Mitigations
  • Choose higher-cardinality keys.
  • Introduce sharding tokens appended to keys to spread load.
  • Use on-demand capacity for unpredictable spikes.
Check your understanding
Which attribute in your app today could cause a hot partition if used as the partition key? Consider its distribution.

screens.title: Create an Item with put_item (Boto3)
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll examine how to create or overwrite items using the Boto3 resource interface. The put operation accepts an Item object; if an item with the same primary key exists, it will be replaced. This makes put useful for full writes but risky when you want to change only a single attribute. In the provided example you will see a Products table where a product is created with a ProductId, name, description, price and status. Notice how numeric values should be passed as Decimal to avoid floating-point issues in DynamoDB. A typical pattern is to use put for initial inserts or when you intentionally want to replace the item. A common misconception is assuming put_item is always cheaper than update_item; in fact, put_item writes the entire item and can consume more write capacity if the item is large. For incremental changes, prefer update_item which modifies specific attributes. After running a put, verify by reading the item with a get operation. Try this sequence locally: create the table, put two items, then fetch one to confirm its attributes. Create an Item with put_item (Boto3) means put_item creates or overwrites an item; use decimal for numeric attributes and prefer update_item for partial changes.. In practical terms, use the resource interface to insert or overwrite items safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: put_item creates or overwrites an item; use Decimal for numeric attributes and prefer update_item for partial changes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › put_item
Example: create_product()
This code shows the typical put_item call using the resource Table object.
import boto3
from decimal import Decimal

dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='us-east-1')
table = dynamodb.Table('Products')

response = table.put_item(
  Item={
    'ProductId': 'P001',
    'Name': 'Laptop',
    'Description': 'High-performance laptop',
    'Price': Decimal('1200.00'),
    'Status': 'Available'
  }
)
print('Product created or updated')
Key Takeaway
Use put_item for full item writes. Validate attribute types like Decimal for numbers.
Common Mistake
Using put_item for small changes can waste write capacity by rewriting the entire item.
Why Decimal matters
DynamoDB expects precise numeric types. Using Decimal preserves exact values and avoids floating-point rounding differences when stored and retrieved.
Example verification
After putting the item, call get_item with the ProductId to confirm attributes and types. This verifies the put completed successfully.
Check your understanding
When would you prefer update_item over put_item? Answer: when changing only a subset of attributes to save write capacity and avoid accidental overwrites.

screens.title: Read and Query: get_item and Query Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Reading data in DynamoDB is primarily a primary-key operation. The most efficient way to fetch a single item is to use get_item and supply the full primary key. This returns the exact item with minimal cost and predictable performance. When you need multiple related items, use Query with a partition key and optional sort-key conditions. For example, if you modeled user events with UserID as the partition and Timestamp as the sort key, a query for a specific user and a time range returns ordered events efficiently. The SDK get_item example retrieves a product by ProductId. A misconception to avoid is trying to use scan for routine queries; scan examines every item in a table and is expensive. Scans are acceptable for occasional maintenance or small tables but not for application access patterns. Also, remember that reads have size limits for RCUs: a strongly consistent read of an item up to 4KB consumes one RCU. If you can tolerate eventual consistency, you can often halve read capacity usage with eventually consistent reads. After reading, consider whether the access pattern should be supported by a global secondary index or rethought at the primary key level.

keyIdea.text: Use get_item for single-item lookups by full primary key; use Query for grouped, ordered retrievals by partition and sort key. Avoid scan for frequent access.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › get_item & Query
get_item example
def get_product(product_id):
  response = table.get_item(
    Key={ 'ProductId': product_id }
  )
  return response.get('Item')

# Efficient single-item retrieval
Use get_item when you have the full primary key. It's the most efficient read and minimizes RCUs.
Query example (conceptual)
Query for all items with the same partition key, optionally limiting by sort key conditions like a timestamp range. Results are returned in sorted order when using a sort key.
Best Practice
Prefer Query for grouped reads, reserve Scan for occasional maintenance tasks, and choose eventual consistency where acceptable to reduce RCUs.

screens.title: Update and Delete with update_item and delete_item
screens.narratorSegment: Updating and deleting items are common operations that, when used properly, save throughput and avoid accidental data loss. update_item lets you modify specific attributes with an update expression. Because it changes parts of an item rather than replacing it, update_item can be more efficient than put_item for small changes. The example shows updating the price and using ExpressionAttributeNames to avoid reserved-word conflicts. Always request updated attributes back when you need confirmation by using ReturnValues set to updated attributes. For deletes, delete_item requires the full primary key to remove the item. A common misconception is thinking update_item always creates fewer write units; the write capacity consumed depends on the final size of the item and the attributes changed. Also ensure your application handles conditional updates if you need optimistic concurrency. After an update or delete, verify with a subsequent get operation. Use these operations to implement safe, minimal-change workflows in your application. Update and Delete with update_item and delete_item means use update_item for targeted attribute changes and delete_item with a full primary key to remove items safely.. In practical terms, modify specific attributes and remove items without full rewrites. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › update_item & delete_item
update_item example
from decimal import Decimal

response = table.update_item(
  Key={ 'ProductId': 'P001' },
  UpdateExpression="SET Price = :p",
  ExpressionAttributeValues={ ':p': Decimal('1250.00') },
  ReturnValues="UPDATED_NEW"
)
print('Updated attributes:', response.get('Attributes'))
Use ExpressionAttributeNames when updating attributes that are reserved words. ReturnValues lets you inspect what changed.
delete_item example
response = table.delete_item(
  Key={ 'ProductId': 'P002' }
)
print('Delete response:', response)
Best Practice
Use conditional expressions if you want to prevent accidental overwrites or deletes based on item state. Confirm changes with get_item when necessary.

screens.title: Capacity Models: Provisioned vs On-Demand and RCUs/WCUs
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB supports provisioned capacity and on-demand capacity. Under provisioned mode you set Read Capacity Units and Write Capacity Units. One RCU equals one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads. One WCU equals one write per second for an item up to one kilobyte. These units let you predict costs and cap throughput, but if your estimates are low you will see throttling. On-demand capacity eliminates the need to pre-provision by scaling automatically for variable traffic, which simplifies operations but may be more costly for steady, predictable workloads. A common operational mistake is over-provisioning to avoid throttling, which increases cost; under-provisioning yields ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exceptions. Monitor capacity metrics and use autoscaling policies to adapt. For example, if your application performs frequent small writes under 1KB, each write consumes one WCU; multiply expected writes per second by that amount to size the table. Choose on-demand for erratic spikes and provisioned for stable high-volume traffic with autoscaling to balance cost and availability. In practical terms, understand throughput units and their operational trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Capacity & Throttling
RCUs and WCUs
Throughput units map to item sizes and consistency models.
Read Capacity Unit (RCU)
One RCU = one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to 4KB. Two eventually consistent reads fit one RCU.
Write Capacity Unit (WCU)
One WCU = one write per second for an item up to 1KB. Larger items consume proportionally more WCUs.
Provisioned vs On-Demand
Choose based on traffic predictability and cost sensitivity.
Provisioned
Set RCUs/WCUs and optionally enable autoscaling. Predictable performance and cost when traffic is steady.
On-Demand
Automatic scaling for variable or unpredictable traffic. Simplifies operations but can cost more under steady load.
Operational alert
ProvisionedThroughputExceededException means your RCUs or WCUs are too low. Increase capacity or switch to on-demand to mitigate immediate throttling.

screens.title: Data Modeling Mistakes and Mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Developers often make predictable mistakes when moving from relational thinking to a key-driven NoSQL model. First, hot partitions happen when a partition key has low cardinality or a few values receive most traffic. This is often visible as throttling despite low overall table capacity. Mitigation strategies include choosing a more distributed partition attribute, introducing artificial sharding tokens, or using on-demand capacity for irregular spikes. Second, reserved words can break update expressions; use ExpressionAttributeNames to avoid conflicts. Third, numeric handling: DynamoDB stores numbers as exact types, so use Decimal in Python to preserve precision. Fourth, over-reliance on scan for queries leads to high read costs; migrate to Query with appropriate keys or secondary indexes. Finally, over-provisioning capacity simply to avoid throttling inflates cost; use autoscaling policies to adapt to traffic patterns. For each pitfall, there is a practical countermeasure. After you identify the issue in your app, choose the least invasive fix first, then consider architectural changes like introducing new partitioning or indexes. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Pitfalls & Fixes
Hot partitions
Cause: low-cardinality partition keys or uneven request distribution. Fix: choose higher-cardinality keys, shard keys, or use on-demand for spikes.
Reserved words
Cause: using attribute names that conflict with DynamoDB syntax in update expressions. Fix: use ExpressionAttributeNames to alias fields.
Numeric types
Cause: using floating-point types. Fix: use Decimal for precise numeric storage from Python.
Excessive scans
Cause: querying without a suitable key or index. Fix: model keys for access patterns or add a secondary index where needed.
Capacity mismatch
Cause: under- or over-provisioning RCUs/WCUs. Fix: monitor metrics and enable autoscaling or switch to on-demand when appropriate.
Overwrites from put_item
Cause: using put_item when only partial changes are needed. Fix: prefer update_item for partial modifications to avoid accidental data loss.

First, a Table stores Items made of Attributes; DynamoDB is schema-less so item shapes can vary, but keys must be consistent. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore Amazon DynamoDB from a developer's point of view. We'll build a clear mental model: DynamoDB stores tables of items made of attributes and uses primary keys to find data quickly. You'll learn why DynamoDB is schema-less, when that flexibility helps, and why choosing the right partition key prevents performance issues. We'll also cover how the AWS SDK performs basic create, read, update and delete operations, and how capacity—read and write units—affects cost and throttling. For example, you will see how a Products table can store different attributes per item without breaking queries, and how using a user identifier plus timestamp supports efficient event retrieval. We'll contrast on-demand capacity and provisioned RCUs/WCUs so you understand operational trade-offs. By the end of the chapter you will be able to model a simple table, perform CRUD with Boto3, and spot common design mistakes like low-cardinality keys that create hot partitions. Consider what access patterns your app needs before you choose a primary key; that choice will guide your entire design.

In these objectives we translate chapter goals into developer skills you can use right away. First, you'll grasp DynamoDB's building blocks—tables, items, attributes, and primary keys—so you can model entities like products or user events. Second, you'll understand the difference between partition keys and sort keys and how they influence storage and query patterns; for instance, a user identifier plus timestamp lets you fetch a user's activities in order. Third, you'll learn to provision and manage read and write capacity units; this helps you avoid throttling and controls cost. Fourth, you'll perform CRUD operations using the AWS SDK so your application can create, read, update, and delete items predictably. Each objective includes a small competency milestone so you know when you've internalized the skill. For example, after practicing Boto3 calls you should be able to insert an item and update a numeric attribute using the Decimal type. Think about which application access patterns matter for your project before choosing keys. That choice will govern both performance and cost.

This second objectives screen turns chapter outcomes into developer-ready tasks you can verify. First, model primary keys for different access patterns: design a Products table keyed by ProductId for instant lookups, and design an Orders table keyed by CustomerID plus OrderDate to fetch a customer's history. Second, practice provisioning capacity: calculate RCUs and WCUs for your typical item size, and experiment with on-demand mode versus provisioned mode with autoscaling. Third, implement CRUD flows using Boto3 resource or client interfaces; learn the difference so you can choose the right abstraction for your use case. Fourth, identify and remediate common pitfalls such as hot partitions, numeric type handling, and accidental overwrites from put_item. Each card below includes a small mnemonic or scenario to help you remember the skill; use the milestones to confirm competency by running the provided hands-on steps. These tasks prepare you to make practical design trade-offs in production systems.

Let's define the core building blocks of DynamoDB so you can map application objects to storage. A table is a container for items. An item is a collection of attributes; think of an item as a document or a row whose attributes can vary from item to item. DynamoDB is schema-less, which means you do not need to define every attribute up front. This flexibility lets you add fields for some items without altering the entire table. However, it also shifts responsibility to you: design your access patterns so important attributes are present where queries expect them. The primary key uniquely identifies each item. If you use a single partition key, DynamoDB hashes its value to choose a storage partition. With a composite primary key—partition and sort—you group related items by partition and order them by the sort key, enabling efficient range queries. A common example is user events: a UserID partition key and a Timestamp sort key let you fetch recent events in chronological order. A misconception is thinking schema-less means structure-free; you still need consistent keys and predictable access paths. What part of your data needs ordered access, and which fields will vary per item?

Primary keys define how DynamoDB stores and finds items, so choosing them is a design decision with operational consequences. When you use a partition key alone, DynamoDB applies an internal hash to the key value to determine the physical partition. This works best when key values are high-cardinality and evenly distributed. With a composite key—partition plus sort—you group related items under the same partition and order them by the sort key, which enables efficient range queries such as retrieving a user's activities by timestamp. A common mistake is picking a low-cardinality partition key such as a fixed status value, which funnels traffic to a few partitions and causes hot partitions. Hot partitions lead to throttling and uneven performance. To choose keys, follow a simple process: first list your access patterns; second identify attributes used to retrieve related sets of items; third prefer attributes with many distinct values for the partition key; fourth use sort keys to support ordered queries or multiple items per partition. For example, to fetch all orders for a customer in order date, choose CustomerID as partition and OrderDate as sort. Reflect on your app: which queries require grouping, and which require single-item lookup?

Now we'll examine how to create or overwrite items using the Boto3 resource interface. The put operation accepts an Item object; if an item with the same primary key exists, it will be replaced. This makes put useful for full writes but risky when you want to change only a single attribute. In the provided example you will see a Products table where a product is created with a ProductId, name, description, price and status. Notice how numeric values should be passed as Decimal to avoid floating-point issues in DynamoDB. A typical pattern is to use put for initial inserts or when you intentionally want to replace the item. A common misconception is assuming put_item is always cheaper than update_item; in fact, put_item writes the entire item and can consume more write capacity if the item is large. For incremental changes, prefer update_item which modifies specific attributes. After running a put, verify by reading the item with a get operation. Try this sequence locally: create the table, put two items, then fetch one to confirm its attributes. Create an Item with put_item (Boto3) means put_item creates or overwrites an item; use decimal for numeric attributes and prefer update_item for partial changes.. In practical terms, use the resource interface to insert or overwrite items safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reading data in DynamoDB is primarily a primary-key operation. The most efficient way to fetch a single item is to use get_item and supply the full primary key. This returns the exact item with minimal cost and predictable performance. When you need multiple related items, use Query with a partition key and optional sort-key conditions. For example, if you modeled user events with UserID as the partition and Timestamp as the sort key, a query for a specific user and a time range returns ordered events efficiently. The SDK get_item example retrieves a product by ProductId. A misconception to avoid is trying to use scan for routine queries; scan examines every item in a table and is expensive. Scans are acceptable for occasional maintenance or small tables but not for application access patterns. Also, remember that reads have size limits for RCUs: a strongly consistent read of an item up to 4KB consumes one RCU. If you can tolerate eventual consistency, you can often halve read capacity usage with eventually consistent reads. After reading, consider whether the access pattern should be supported by a global secondary index or rethought at the primary key level.

Updating and deleting items are common operations that, when used properly, save throughput and avoid accidental data loss. update_item lets you modify specific attributes with an update expression. Because it changes parts of an item rather than replacing it, update_item can be more efficient than put_item for small changes. The example shows updating the price and using ExpressionAttributeNames to avoid reserved-word conflicts. Always request updated attributes back when you need confirmation by using ReturnValues set to updated attributes. For deletes, delete_item requires the full primary key to remove the item. A common misconception is thinking update_item always creates fewer write units; the write capacity consumed depends on the final size of the item and the attributes changed. Also ensure your application handles conditional updates if you need optimistic concurrency. After an update or delete, verify with a subsequent get operation. Use these operations to implement safe, minimal-change workflows in your application. Update and Delete with update_item and delete_item means use update_item for targeted attribute changes and delete_item with a full primary key to remove items safely.. In practical terms, modify specific attributes and remove items without full rewrites. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DynamoDB supports provisioned capacity and on-demand capacity. Under provisioned mode you set Read Capacity Units and Write Capacity Units. One RCU equals one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to four kilobytes, or two eventually consistent reads. One WCU equals one write per second for an item up to one kilobyte. These units let you predict costs and cap throughput, but if your estimates are low you will see throttling. On-demand capacity eliminates the need to pre-provision by scaling automatically for variable traffic, which simplifies operations but may be more costly for steady, predictable workloads. A common operational mistake is over-provisioning to avoid throttling, which increases cost; under-provisioning yields ProvisionedThroughputExceeded exceptions. Monitor capacity metrics and use autoscaling policies to adapt.
